meta.tagline: The Arctic Circle, Santa's village and lights that dance across the sky

overview.title: Welcome to Rovaniemi
overview.intro: Rovaniemi is the crossing point of two fairytales: one wears a red coat and a beard and is world-famous; the other dances across the sky in green curtains. But this city is more than fairytale — flattened in the war, reborn from Alvar Aalto's pen in the shape of a reindeer's antlers, it is a Lapland capital with its feet on the ground. In winter the snow swallows every sound; in summer the sun never sets. Fill your thermos and dress in layers: here nature is not the tourist but the host.

local_word.definition: Finnish's untranslatable word: quiet, stubborn determination in the face of hardship. Watch a Rovaniemi local cycling through minus 25 with a smile and you'll understand what it means.

rules.title: Respect the cold, trust the layers
rules.description: Minus 20 is normal in winter: wool not cotton, three thin layers not one thick one. With the base layer + fleece + windproof shell formula every activity becomes a joy; to the badly dressed, the city closes its doors.

rules.title: The aurora isn't guaranteed — it demands patience
rules.description: The revontulet (northern lights) can appear from late August to April, but clouds and luck are part of the game. Stay at least 3-4 nights, follow the aurora forecast apps, and never be too lazy to step outside at midnight.

rules.title: The sauna is sacred, and it has its rules
rules.description: You enter a Finnish sauna with a towel, not a swimsuit; you shower first; silence is appreciated. If you have the courage, follow the sauna with the ice hole (avanto): your heart leaps to your throat, then you live the most alive five minutes of your life.

quick_facts.label: Airport
quick_facts.sub: 10 min to centre · 1h20 flight from Helsinki

quick_facts.label: Signature
quick_facts.sub: The Arctic Circle line runs through it

tip.label: The Rovaniemi philosophy
tip.text: Here the boss is not your schedule but the weather: if the sky is clear, cancel every plan and go hunt the lights; if it's overcast, make it a museum and sauna day. Flexibility is the most valuable thing in any Lapland suitcase.

transport.title: Getting Around
transport.intro: The centre is small enough to walk; the real question is getting to the village, the farms and the darkness of the forest. The plan is simple: on foot in town, bus or tour transfer beyond it.

items.title: Airport to the centre
items.description: The airport is 10 minutes from town: the airport bus is synced with flights and drops you at your hotel, and taxis run close to a flat rate. In winter the cold greets you the moment you step off the plane — carry your coat in your hand, not your suitcase.

items.title: Bus number 8 — the Santa express
items.description: The local number 8 reaches Santa Claus Village from the centre in half an hour, at half the price of the tourist shuttle. Check the return times — evening departures thin out.

items.title: The centre on foot
items.description: Everything between Lordi Square, the Arktikum and the riverside is within 15 minutes. In winter the pavements are snowy but well kept; ice-grip boots or slip-on spikes are lifesavers.

items.title: Tour transfers — the night hunt
items.description: Most aurora, husky and reindeer tours pick you up from your hotel: heading into the dark forest alone without a car is hard in winter, and a good night tour means a driver + photographer + thermos.

items.title: A rental car — the free hunt
items.description: If you drive, a rental with winter tyres means freedom on the aurora hunt: you can chase a gap in the clouds 100 km away. Experience on snowy roads is essential, and reindeer by the roadside are a genuine traffic factor.

callout.label: Ticket tip
callout.text: Entry to Santa Claus Village is free — the money is in the photos and activities. Take bus 8, chat with Santa (free), and decide on the photo package there.

stay.title: Where to Stay
stay.intro: In Rovaniemi the choice is binary: stay in town and head out on tours — or take a glass igloo or cabin in the forest and let the lights come to you.

local_word.definition: The polar night: the period in December when the sun never rises and the sky hangs in a blue-violet twilight even at noon. Not darkness — an indescribable state of light the Finns call the 'blue moment'.

items.name: The city centre
items.description: Restaurants, supermarkets and tour departure points within walking distance: a wide range from budget hotels to design hotels. The easiest base for aurora tours.

items.name: Around Santa Claus Village
items.description: Igloo hotels and cabins right by the village: a dream for families with children, exactly right for waking up on the Arctic Circle. 8 km from town — plan your dinners in advance.

items.name: Ounasvaara hill
items.description: The forested hill across the river: ski slopes, hiking trails and a sky far from the city lights. 20 minutes from the centre over the bridge — a balance of nature and town.

items.name: The riverside — Kemijoki
items.description: Hotels and apartments along the Kemijoki: in summer the midnight sun strikes the river, in winter the frozen river becomes a walking track. Close to the centre but calm.

items.name: Forest cabins and igloo resorts
items.description: Glass-roofed igloos and fireplace cabins outside town: watching the northern lights from your bed is expensive but unforgettable. Consider it for at least one night, and spend the rest in town.

best_time.title: When to Go
best_time.intro: There are two different cities in Rovaniemi: the snowy fairytale city and the green city of the unsetting sun. Both are real, and they are nothing alike.

items.label: Spring
items.name: Bright Snow
items.subtitle: Spring · Sunny snow, lengthening days
items.description: March is winter's best-kept secret: the snow is still metres deep, but the sun shows its face and the daytime cold softens. The peak month for the aurora + snow activities + sunshine combination. In May the snow melts and the river wakes.

callout.label: March tip
callout.text: The weeks around the March equinox are the statistical peak of aurora activity: high chances at night, sunbathing on snow by day. This is winter in its comfortable form.

items.label: Summer
items.name: The Midnight Sun
items.subtitle: Summer · The sun never sets, 6 June–7 July
items.description: For a month the sun never dips below the horizon: people paddle the river at two in the morning, the forest smells of bilberries, and the mosquitoes join the party. Prices are low, nature is endless — an entirely different Lapland.

callout.label: July tip
callout.text: Walk up Ounasvaara at midnight: at 00.00 the sun touches the horizon and climbs again. Look with your eyes before the camera — this light exists in no filter.

items.label: Autumn
items.name: Ruska and First Lights
items.subtitle: Autumn · Golden forest, first auroras
items.description: In September the forest turns to 'ruska' colours: gold, copper, crimson. The nights darken and the aurora season opens — with friendly prices before the snow tourism begins. November is the month of darkness and waiting for snow.

callout.label: September tip
callout.text: September is the hidden champion: the auroras begin, the lakes haven't frozen yet, and the lights reflect on the water. No crowds, double the show.

items.label: Winter
items.name: Fairytale Season
items.subtitle: Winter · Kaamos twilight, Christmas peak
items.description: December is Santa's main stage: the village glitters, and prices and crowds peak with it. January and February are the real winter: minus twenties, thick falling snow, husky sleds and long aurora nights.

callout.label: December note
callout.text: For Christmas week book everything months ahead: hotel, tours, even restaurants. If you want the same fairytale at half price, pick mid-January — the snow is the same snow, and Santa is still at his desk.

eat.title: What to Eat
eat.intro: Lapland's kitchen comes from the forest and the river: reindeer, salmon, wild berries and coffee brewed over fire. Simple, honest and designed for the cold.

local_word.definition: Lapland's national dish: thinly shaved reindeer sautéed in butter, served with mashed potatoes and lingonberry jam. Be surprised by the meat-and-sweet balance, then wipe the plate clean.

items.name: Poronkäristys — sautéed reindeer
items.description: The classic, served with mash, pickles and lingonberries: reindeer is lean, tender and sustainable — the millennia-old inheritance of Sámi herding. The mandatory plate of your first Lapland evening.
items.tag: At a classic restaurant · with lingonberries

items.name: Lohikeitto — salmon soup
items.description: Creamy salmon soup with dill and rye bread: step in from minus 20 and this is the best dish on earth. Simmered daily in the riverside restaurants.

items.name: Leipäjuusto — the squeaky cheese
items.description: 'Bread cheese': slices of baked fresh cheese served warm, topped with amber-orange cloudberry (lakka) jam. The squeak against your teeth is the mark of quality.

items.name: Forest berries and the market stalls
items.description: In late summer the markets pile up with bilberries, lingonberries and golden cloudberries: under Finland's 'everyman's right' (jokamiehenoikeus) you're free to pick them in the forest yourself — grab a basket.
items.tag: Late summer · from market or forest

items.name: Nokipannu coffee by the fire
items.description: Smoke-scented 'nokipannu' coffee is brewed over an open fire, with a fire-roasted makkara (sausage) alongside: the kota (Lapp tent) break in the middle of every snow tour exists for this ritual.
items.tag: On a tour break · in a kota tent

items.name: Lapin Kulta and cloudberry liqueur
items.description: The north's beer, Lapin Kulta ('Lapland gold'), is plain and cold; the after-dinner lakka liqueur is the cloudberry's sweet farewell. Between the two sits a courage test flavoured with pine tar.

callout.label: Budget tip
callout.text: Finland's lunch menu (lounas) culture is generous: on weekdays from 11 to 2 the same restaurants serve soup + main + coffee at half the evening price. Make lunch your big meal.

hidden_gems.title: Hidden Corners
hidden_gems.intro: Everyone finds Santa; these six are Rovaniemi's quiet side.

items.name: Arktikum
items.description: The museum whose glass tunnel reaches towards the river is where Arctic life and Lapland's history are best told: the city burned in the war, Sámi culture, the science of the aurora. Sit at the end of the glass corridor facing the river — on many winter nights the lights have been watched from inside the museum itself.

items.name: Jätkänkynttilä bridge
items.description: The 'Lumberjack's Candle' bridge rises over the Kemijoki with its flame sculpture: at sunset its silhouette from the riverbank is the city's signature. In winter the walking track on the frozen river passes beneath it.

items.rarity: A town plan shaped like antlers
items.name: The Aalto centre and Lappia House
items.description: After the war Alvar Aalto drew the city on the plan of a reindeer's antlers; his library, theatre (Lappia) and town hall still stand. The library's light-welled reading room is the city's warmest refuge at minus 25.

items.name: The Ounasvaara summit trail
items.description: Cross the bridge and you're at the summit in half an hour: copper-coloured paths in summer, snowshoe routes in winter, and aurora spots with their backs to the city lights. The observation tower at the top is built for sunrise.

items.name: Korundi House of Culture
items.description: A contemporary art museum converted from an old post-bus depot: one of the best collections of northern art and home of the Lapland Chamber Orchestra. Exactly right as a snowstorm-day plan.

items.rarity: First step into the ice hole
items.name: Avanto — the ice swimming clubs
items.description: The local swimming clubs cut ice holes in the river each winter: try the sauna + avanto combination not as a tourist package but in its real form, alongside the locals. Shyness stays at the door; screaming is allowed.

callout.label: Aurora tip
callout.text: If you want to see the lights without leaving town, the rule is simple: turn your back to the city lights. The frozen surface of the river, the foot of Ounasvaara and the far bank by the bridge — all three are dark spots within walking distance.

traps.title: Tourist Traps
traps.intro: Rovaniemi sells a fairytale; inside the fairytale there is also an invoice. Arrive knowing these four.

items.name: The Santa photo package shock
items.description: Meeting Santa is free, but shooting with your own phone is forbidden; at the exit the photo packages arrive with surprising prices.
items.instead: Meet first, choose the package after: even a single digital frame carries the memory. Skip the video-and-album bundles, take the small one, and save the budget for the husky tour.

items.name: The 10-minute 'safari'
items.description: Some husky and reindeer 'safaris' last half a day including hotel pickup — but the time on the sled is 10 minutes; the brochure says so in small print.
items.instead: Before booking, ask plainly: 'how many minutes/km on the sled?' Good farms give real 5-10 km runs plus a farm tour — the difference is made not by price, but by asking.

items.name: 'Guaranteed aurora' marketing
items.description: No tour can guarantee the northern lights; 'guarantee' usually means 'a free second tour if not seen' — which under cloud ends the same way.
items.instead: Choose small-group tours that read cloud maps and change route, and spread your chances over 3-4 nights. Smile at any package promising auroras to a one-night visitor, and walk on.

items.name: Staying at the Village and eating every meal there
items.description: Santa Claus Village restaurants are priced for a captive audience: an ordinary salmon soup costs double the town price.
items.instead: Plan your meals in the town centre or around lounas menus, and arrive at the village fed. If you're staying in an igloo hotel, calculate the half-board price beforehand.

callout.label: Golden rule
callout.text: In Lapland every activity has two versions: the one for the busloads, and the way locals do it. Never hesitate to ask the price and 'how big is the group?' — two questions that double the quality of the trip.

itinerary.title: Ready-Made Routes
itinerary.intro: If you hate planning, follow these flows. The times are flexible; keep the spirit, break the order. (Winter version — in summer, swap the aurora hunt for the midnight sun.)

plans.title: If You Have 1 Day
plans.subtitle: A concentrated fairytale on the Arctic Circle

steps.title: Breakfast + layer up
steps.description: A solid breakfast in the centre, three layers of clothing on top: you're mostly outdoors today. Don't forget to fill the thermos.

steps.title: Santa Claus Village
steps.description: Bus 8 to the village: take a real step across the Arctic Circle line, collect your certificate, chat with Santa and post your card with the Arctic Circle postmark.

steps.title: Back to town + lounas
steps.description: A lunch menu in the centre: salmon soup + rye bread. Then a short loop around Lordi Square and a look at the souvenirs.

steps.title: The Arktikum's glass tunnel
steps.description: Dive into Lapland's history and aurora science at the Arctic museum: as it darkens outside (after 3 pm in winter) the glass corridor over the river turns to blue hour.

steps.title: Sauna + avanto courage
steps.description: Warm up in a hotel or public sauna; if you dare, one dip in the ice hole. For dinner, poronkäristys — seal the day Lapland-style.

steps.title: The aurora hunt
steps.description: If the sky is clear: on a tour, or on the frozen riverbank with your back to the town. If the green curtain opens, put the camera down — watch with bare eyes first.

plans.title: If You Have 3 Days
plans.subtitle: Fairytale, forest and ice, in turn

steps.title: Classic Rovaniemi
steps.description: The one-day flow above: village, Arktikum, sauna, first aurora hunt.

steps.title: Husky and reindeer day
steps.description: A real 5-10 km sled run at a husky farm in the morning; afternoon tea with Sámi stories at a reindeer farm; evening a fireside dinner in a kota tent and a second aurora watch.

steps.title: Ounasvaara and farewell
steps.description: Snowshoe to the Ounasvaara summit or ski; an art break at Korundi at midday; a farewell table of leipäjuusto + lakka liqueur in the evening. If the sky is clear, one last hunt — the third night is usually the lucky one.

phrases.title: 5-Word Survival Kit
phrases.intro: Finnish is a hard language, but nobody expects you to speak it; these five open doors and smiles.

items.meaning: Hello — say it twice (hei hei) and it becomes goodbye
Thank you — the word you'll use most in Finland
Cheers! — eye contact as the glasses rise is kept Finnish-short
The northern lights — literally 'fox fires': in the legend, the arctic fox sweeps snow with its tail and sets the sky alight
The one Finnish word the whole world borrowed — invented here, and properly pronounced 'sow-nah'
